# Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16 (PTS DN ii 72))

**ID:** DN 16 (PTS DN ii 72)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16) is the longest discourse in the Pali Sutta Piṭaka and provides an extended biographical narrative of the Buddha's final months, decease, and funeral arrangements [Crosby 2014; Piya Tan 2004]. Unlike doctrinal dialogues standard in the Nikāyas, it forms a composite chronicle opening on Vulture Peak near Rājagaha with a discussion of the exemplary republican governance of the Vajjīs, progressing through his journey toward Kusinārā, his mortal illness, and his instruction of his final direct convert, the wanderer Subhadda [Gethin 2001; Collins 1998; Tzungkuen Wen 2009]. Along this narrative course, the discourse integrates fundamental doctrinal syntheses—such as the explicit grouping of the thirty-seven requisites of awakening (*bodhipakkhiya-dhammā*)—as well as descriptions of the causes of earthquakes, instructions for the veneration of bodily relics and the erection of stūpas, and the eventual division of his relics [Gethin 2001; Kingsbury 2002; Winternitz 1933; Gaffney 2003; Crosby 2014]. Along with the Vinaya *Mahāvagga*, it constitutes one of the two earliest and most extensive biographical records preserved in the early Pali canon [Gaffney 2003].

Scholars characterize the text as a composite mosaic that expanded incrementally from an ancient core to its final redaction, incorporating earlier narrative elements alongside newer institutional and cultic developments such as stūpa worship [Winternitz 1933; Nakamura 1980; Piya Tan 2004]. In the commentary tradition, Buddhaghosa's commentary in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī* elucidates its historical and narrative context, which has been translated into English by Yang-Gyu An [Collins 1998; Piya Tan 2004]. The title itself signifies the discourse on the Buddha's "Great Final Extinguishment" (*mahā-parinibbāna*) rather than simply denoting a "great sutta" [Piya Tan 2004].

The sutta is embedded in an exceptionally rich network of parallels across Buddhist traditions, including the Sanskrit *Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra* (preserved in Central Asian Turfan and Gilgit manuscripts), Gāndhārī fragments, four Chinese Āgama translations (notably in the *Dīrghāgama*, DĀ 2, as well as T 5, T 6, and T 7), and the Tibetan translation of the Mūlasarvāstivāda *Vinayakṣudrakavastu*, all extensively analyzed in comparative studies by André Bareau and others [Gethin 2001; Winternitz 1933; Nakamura 1980; Piya Tan 2004]. DharmaNexus strongly aligns the Pali text with the Sanskrit *Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra*, the Tibetan *Vinayakṣudrakavastu*, and the Chinese *Dīrghāgama* (T 1) [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, large narrative sections and doctrinal pericopes are shared directly with the *Aṭṭhakanipāta* (AN 8.70), *Catukkanipāta* (AN 4.180), *Sattakanipāta* (AN 7.22–27), the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* of the Vinaya (Kd 6), the *Iddhipāda Saṁyutta* (SN 51.10), the *Satipaṭṭhāna Saṁyutta* (SN 47.9), and the *Udāna* (Ud 6.1 and Ud 8.5) [DharmaNexus].
